newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli analyst stirs row with coup warning.
newsitem.headline: Israeli analyst stirs row with coup warning.

text.p: Strained relations between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the Israeli military burst out in the open on Wednesday when a leading strategic analyst warned of a heightened chance of a coup.

Israeli politicians and retired generals denied the assertion by Professor Zeev Maoz, head of the Jaffee Centre for Strategic Studies, but spoke of a deep rift between the four-month-old government and the army's top brass.
"I don't think that (a coup) is a possibility," said reserve major-general Amram Mitzna, now mayor of Haifa, Israel's third largest city.
"But the fact is that there is a growing lack of trust between the military and security echelon and the political echelon...It's an impossible situation," he told Israel Radio.

Maoz said Netanyahu considered senior army officers to be aligned with the former Labour government that signed breakthrough peace deals with the Palestinians and Jordan and was ignoring their assessments.
"If we face an international crisis while a lack of trust prevails between the military and political echelons, there are good reasons to be concerned," he told the newspaper Haaretz.

"The military has no opportunity to play the political game in order to change the situation and therefore the likelihood of a putsch -- an illegal action -- becomes more and more attractive," said Maoz, whose centre is one of the country's leading think tanks.
The prime minister's office had no comment.

Relations between the government and some members of the army's general staff have been troubled since Netanyahu, leader fo the right-wing Likud party, ousted the Labour-led government in elections last May.
Netanyahu had accused Labour of politicising the army by appointing officers to help negotiate Israel-PLO peace deals which the Likud leader opposed.

Army chief Lieutenant-General Amnon Shahak traded his army uniform for a suit and tie briefly for talks with Palestinian negotiator Nabil Shaath in 1993 that led to Israel's withdrawal from Gaza and Jericho.

Likud legislator Uzi Landau, who heads the Knesset's powerful Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee, referred to members of the army's general staff earlier this year as "lackeys" of the previous government.

"The prime minister and his immediate circle think senior security officials were all political appointments. Bibi and his people are convinced the army echelon's involvement amounted to a political stand," Maoz said, using Netanyahu's nickname.

Israeli officers have taken part in political decision-making since before the state's founding in 1948 and many have gone into political careers after retiring from the army but the Jewish state has long prided itself on a separation between the military and political branches.
Netanyahu's cabinet includes four retired generals.

"We're an army of conscripts and reserve soldiers, left, right and centre...there's no danger in my opinion of a military putsch," said legislator Ran Cohen of the left-wing Meretz party, a reserve lieutenant-colonel.

Maoz said the government did not consult security officials before opening a second entrance to an archaeological tunnel in Jerusalem's Old City last month that touched off unprecedented gunbattles and clashes in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
